items.title: Wendell Brunious interviewed by Monk Rowe, Scottsdale, Arizona, April 16, 2000 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: When you think of Louis Armstrong himself, the dues that that guy paid that no one had to pay after him. Every jazz musician is standing on Louis Armstrong’s shoulders.

ctx.x: Do you think that some of the younger generation got to the point where they felt the blues was denigrating to their culture?

That’s a good question. That’s a very good question. It could be, but you know my dad used to say to me there’s a reason for everything but there is no excuse for anything. So don’t make that your excuse not to learn the blues. Because the blues is something real. And it’s got a real place in jazz. So I mean you can hey man it’s degrading or it’s Uncle Tom or whatever, I mean it’s just, don’t use the excuse, because of that that’s why I don’t play the blues. When you think of Louis Armstrong himself, the dues…

shoulders. Every one. I mean he didn’t have too many, I mean he had Joe Oliver as a mentor, he had a few guys, B.A. Rolfe that he heard play, but he pretty much single- handedly revolutionized jazz and just did the whole thing man. Everything after him was affected by him. He and like Michaelangelo are like two of the greatest artists. I mean the world just was not the same after these guys. And I mean this is before mass media. Oh man, Louis Armstrong, I mean to be a black man, and I’m not talking a Creole man…

items.title: Wendell Brunious interviewed by Michael Woods, Los Angeles, California, September 3, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: I was sitting there in admiration of your comments, especially about Louis Armstrong, who, without him, I really don’t know what position jazz would be

ctx.x: I was sitting there in admiration of your comments, especially about Louis Armstrong, who, without him, I really don’t know what position jazz would be — I don’t know if there would even be jazz actually.

Well I know you’ll agree it’s kind of sad that even accomplished, even many accomplished jazz musicians don’t fully understand what Louis did for the music you know. And they give him a lot of lip service and say oh Pops, oh yeah, Satchmo, yeah Louis, yeah, right. And I don’t think that many of them have actually checked out those records.
